2611.26785.title: SciPIC-lite: A flexible Halo Occupation Distribution pipeline aimed at clustering observables

2611.26785.abstract: The Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework provides a flexible approach to modelling the galaxy--halo connection in cosmological simulations, encoding the statistical relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter haloes. We present SciPIC-lite, a new public Python library for fast, flexible, and user-friendly HOD modelling, designed to populate dark matter haloes extracted from cosmological simulations with galaxies and to provide a comprehensive suite of tools for their subsequent analysis. The library is built around a modular and extensible codebase that incorporates the full breadth of the HOD framework, from the core occupation functions to a wide range of physically motivated extensions, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of galaxy clustering applications. We validate and characterise the performance of SciPIC-lite by developing a pipeline to fit the two-point correlation functions of H$\alpha$-selected galaxies from the Flagship~2 simulation across multiple redshift bins. To this end, we populate AbacusSummit dark matter haloes with galaxies according to a variety of HOD parametrisations. We assess the robustness of the fits with respect to the choice of HOD parametrisation and the inclusion of physically motivated extensions, including assembly bias, velocity bias, conformity, and halo profile rescaling. The best-fit models are found to be remarkably robust across different HOD parametrisations and fitting configurations, with reduced $\chi^2$ values clustering tightly around a common value regardless of the model adopted. We exploit these results to generate new AbacusSummit-based galaxy mocks that accurately reproduce the clustering properties of the Flagship~2 H$\alpha$ galaxy population.

2611.26822.title: Kinetic Sunyaev Zel'dovich Velocity Reconstruction Using Vision Transformers

figures.caption: Figure 1: $T$he Vision Transformer (ViT)-based kSZ $v$elocity reconstruction pipeline. In the top panel, full-sky $N_{\rm side}=2048$ HEALPix maps are split into 12 $2048\times 2048$ pixel faces, then each face is split into tiles of $256\times 256$ pixels which are the inputs to the ViT. In the bottom panel, 4 channels of tiles (one integrated T tile and 3 binned $\tau$ tiles) are passed through the patch embedding to the Transformer Encoder Block consisting of Multi-Head Self Attention and MLP layers with Layer Norm, and then passed through the MLP Output head to the 3 channel output of binned v tiles.

Figure 2: Training loss curves for random Gaussian mock data in the Vision Transformer (ViT) for combined (top), pixel (bottom left), patch (bottom center), and spectral (bottom right) losses. Plots show the train (blue) and test (orange) losses across epochs. Stages transitions (vertical grey dotted) take the weights from the epoch with the minimum loss (star) and discard the unused epochs (red shading).

Figure 3: The correlation coefficient $r_{\ell}$ between the true underlying velocity field in bin 2 for random Gaussian mock data and the quadratic estimator (QE) evaluated with (red) and without (orange) the primary CMB as well as the trained Vision Transformer (ViT) network with (blue) and without (purple) the primary CMB in the input. Shaded regions indicate the cosmic variance error bar. In the absence of the primary CMB, the ViT outperforms the QE. In the presence of the primary CMB, the QE outperforms the ViT.

Figure 4: The correlation coefficient $r_{\ell}$ between the true underlying velocity field in bin 2 for FLAMINGO data with (right panel) and without (left panel) the primary CMB in the input for the quadratic estimator (QE, red), the Vision Transformer without finetuning on FLAMINGO data (ViT Base, blue), and the Vision Transformer with finetuning on rotated FLAMINGO data (ViT Finetuned, purple). Shaded regions indicate the cosmic variance error bars. The finetuned ViT is able to use non-Gaussian information in the inputs to produce a superior reconstruction, in particular on small angular scales.

Figure 4: The correlation coefficient $r_{\ell}$ between the true underlying velocity field in bin 2 for FLAMINGO data with (right panel) and without (left panel) the primary CMB in the input for the quadratic estimator (QE, red), the Vision Transformer without finetuning on FLAMINGO data (ViT Base, blue), and the Vision Transformer with finetuning on rotated FLAMINGO data (ViT Finetuned, purple). Shaded regions indicate the cosmic variance error bars. The finetuned ViT is able to use non-Gaussian information in the inputs to produce a superior reconstruction, in particular on small angular scales.

Figure 5: The true (left) and reconstructed (middle and right) radial velocity field in Bin 0 for a random Gaussian validation sample with $\epsilon=0$ (no primary CMB in the input, top row) and $\epsilon=1$ (full primary CMB in the input, bottom row). The reconstruction with the QE is shown in the middle and the reconstruction with the trained ViT is shown on the right. In both cases, features in the reconstructions are visibly correlated with the true radial velocity maps. There is an increase in reconstruction noise for the QE at $\epsilon=1$ while the amplitude of fluctuations in the ViT reconstruction stays the same, but features de-correlate with the true map.
Figure 6: Same as Fig. 5 but for Bin 1.
Figure 7: Same as Fig. 5 but for Bin 2.

Figure 8: The correlation coefficient between the random Gaussian true radial velocity and the reconstructions in Bin 0 (left) and Bin 1 (right); the corresponding plot for Bin 2 is shown in the main text as Fig. 3. Shaded regions indicate cosmic variance on the measurement, as defined by Eq. (6). For $\epsilon=0$ the ViT outperforms the QE, while for $\epsilon=1$ the QE outperforms the ViT.

Correlation coefficients for the QE and ViT are shown for $\epsilon=0$ (orange, purple) and for $\epsilon=1$ (red, blue). Shaded regions indicate cosmic variance on the measurement, as defined by Eq. (6). For $\epsilon=0$ the ViT outperforms the QE, while for $\epsilon=1$ the QE outperforms the ViT.

2611.26822.abstract: Kinetic Sunyaev Zel'dovich (kSZ) velocity reconstruction uses correlations between maps of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and a tracer of large scale structure (LSS) to infer the large-scale peculiar velocity field. Standard approaches to kSZ velocity reconstruction use quadratic estimators that are Fisher optimal for purely Gaussian fields. Here, we develop a pipeline for kSZ velocity reconstruction based on Vision Transformers (ViT) and show that this approach can improve the fidelity of velocity reconstruction. This is consistent with the network utilizing non-Gaussian information in the inputs that the quadratic estimators do not, though with the single simulation realization we have access to, we cannot exclude overfitting. Our approach can be applied to full-resolution maps from existing and near-term CMB and LSS datasets.

2611.26864.title: Information-Criterion-Driven, Non-linear Deprojection of Angular Imaging Systematics for the SPHEREx Galaxy Clustering Sample

with individual realizations shown in light blue and the mean in

2611.26864.abstract: Imaging systematics that inject false, or suppress true, galaxy clustering signals are of primary concern for current- and next-generation galaxy surveys, such as the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx) in its search for local primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}$. As statistical errors shrink with growing galaxy samples, systematic rather than statistical uncertainties come to dominate the cosmological error budget. For effects whose spatial patterns are known or well-modelled \emph{a priori}, a common mitigation approach regresses (deprojects) the density variation associated with a known angular template. In this work we present and demonstrate novel aspects of this procedure as will be applied to the SPHEREx galaxy clustering sample. These include flexible -- but, crucially, constrained and interpretable -- non-linear basis regression with polynomial/spline bases, and aggressive information criterion-driven automated template selection with an associated unbiased two-stage regression, using agreement between two independent selectors as a consistency diagnostic. The method automatically selects a template set of minimal-but-sufficient complexity while limiting the number of templates actually regressed, minimising cosmological information loss and making modern additive-plus-multiplicative approaches tractable. We demonstrate these features on SPHEREx-like lognormal mock catalogues with injected contamination of various spatial profiles, amplitudes, and levels of complexity. Principled, signal-preserving deprojection of the kind demonstrated here is a crucial step towards achieving SPHEREx's goal of $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) < 0.5$.

2611.27069.title: Beyond the Peak: Constraining early dark energy with the damping tail

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustrative potentials for AxionEDE (black dashed) and AtR (red solid) in different regions of the $(\alpha,\gamma)$ parameter space. Each panel shows a representative potential shape associated with the indicated region; the correspondence between the potential morphology and the parameter ranges is qualitative rather than exact. The four panels illustrate distinct dynamical behaviors: (a) transient slow-roll, (b) reflection, (c) runaway and (d) asymptotic $\phi^{6}$ oscillations.

Figure 2: Marginalized posterior in the $\log_{10}\alpha$–$\log_{10}\gamma$ plane for AtR, with samples colored by the derived $\log_{10}z_{c}$. The contours enclose the $68\%$ and $95\%$ credible regions, and the gray dashed lines mark $\alpha=1$ and $\gamma=1$. The black dot-dashed line denotes the constant-$\lambda$ relation in (3) for $\lambda\simeq 1.6$, a value close to that at the minimum. Samples near this line separate into $\log_{10}z_{c}\simeq 3.8$ and $3.4$, corresponding to the primary and secondary EDE injections.

Figure 3: Profile likelihood of $\log_{10}\alpha$ for the AtR model. The red and blue points correspond to the $\log_{10}\alpha<0$ and $\log_{10}\alpha\geq 0$ branches, respectively. The star marks the best evaluated AtR point. The dotted horizontal lines indicate the $1\sigma$ and $2\sigma$ thresholds, $\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm prof}=1$ and $4$. The black dot-dashed line denotes the minimum $\chi^{2}$ obtained for AxionEDE. The profile is normalized to the best evaluated AtR point.

Figure 4: Background evolution for AxionEDE, the AtR minimum, and an illustrative double-injection solution associated with the potential morphology in Fig. 1(a). The left panel shows the EDE energy fraction $f_{\rm EDE}$, and the right panel shows the scalar-field evolution. The AxionEDE curve is evaluated using the same cosmological parameters as the AtR minimum.

Figure 4: Background evolution for AxionEDE, the AtR minimum, and an illustrative double-injection solution associated with the potential morphology in Fig. 1(a). The left panel shows the EDE energy fraction $f_{\rm EDE}$, and the right panel shows the scalar-field evolution. The AxionEDE curve is evaluated using the same cosmological parameters as the AtR minimum.

Figure 5: Relative residuals of the lensed CMB TT and EE power spectra ($30<\ell<3500$), relative to the reference AxionEDE model. Blue and vermilion curves represent AtR and AtR(a), respectively, while purple points show the binned Planck NPIPE measurements with $1\sigma$ uncertainties.

Figure 6: Relative residuals of the Weyl potential,
$\Delta\Phi_{\rm W}/\Phi_{\rm W}$, with respect to the AxionEDE reference model, for $k=0.01$, $0.05$, and $0.1\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ from top to bottom.
Figure 7: Marginalized posterior distributions for selected cosmological and scalar-field parameters in AxionEDE and AtR. The contours enclose the 68% and 95% credible regions.

Figure 8: A representative double-peaked EDE evolution illustrating the selection criteria. Orange markers indicate the first two significant peaks, with amplitudes $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$, and the green marker denotes the intervening minimum $f_{\rm v}$. This example satisfies $R_{\rm h}\equiv\min(f_{1},f_{2})/\max(f_{1},f_{2})\simeq 0.711$ and $R_{\rm v}\equiv f_{\rm v}/\min(f_{1},f_{2})\simeq 0.313$.

2611.27069.abstract: Early dark energy is commonly characterized by the amplitude and location of its primary energy-injection peak. We show that its post-peak evolution, which we call the \emph{EDE tail}, provides an additional observable probe of the underlying scalar dynamics and can materially affect its ability to alleviate the Hubble tension. We construct a simple phenomenological framework in which distinct regions of a multiscale scalar potential govern the dynamics at different field scales. As a representative realization, we consider a potential that combines axion-like and $\alpha$-attractor-like regimes, thereby allowing the EDE tail to be reshaped through reflection and asymmetric oscillations. Confronting this framework with cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillation, and supernova observations, we find an improved fit to the high-$\ell$ CMB data together with a higher inferred bestfit $H_0$. Our results show that the EDE tail retains observable information about the underlying scalar potential that is not captured by the conventional peak parameters alone. This provides a complementary route for constructing and observationally distinguishing EDE scenarios, and potentially for further alleviating the Hubble tension.

2611.27151.title: Fast and accurate large-volume Lyman-$α$ forest mocks with three-dimensional U-Net trained on IllustrisTNG and FLAMINGO

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic representation of the anisotropic three-dimensional U-Net architectures used in this work. The two input channels contain the line-of-sight dark-matter density and velocity fields. Each convolutional block contains two $3\times 3\times 3$ convolutions with ReLU activations, while downsampling and upsampling are performed only along the line-of-sight direction using kernels $(2,1,1)$. The TNG and FLAMINGO models use four and three encoder levels, respectively, with bottleneck widths of 192 and 96 channels. Additive skip connections combine the encoder features with the corresponding upsampled decoder features. A final $1\times 1\times 1$ convolution produces a single $\log_{10}\tau$ field, from which the transmitted flux is obtained as $F=\exp(-\tau)$.

Figure 2: Transmitted flux along a randomly chosen skewer in the T$N$G $300\,\mathrm{cMpc}$ test volume: hydrodynamical reference, network predictions from 2LPT and N-body inputs, and FGPA applied to the 2LPT density.

Figure 3: Flux PDF (left) and noiseless 1D power spectrum with ratios to the hydrodynamical reference (right) for the TNG and FLAMINGO test volumes. ML curves are medians over ten uniformly sampled post-burn-in checkpoints, with the 16th–84th percentile checkpoint scatter shaded; hydrodynamical bands show the standard error across independent patches. Both statistics are evaluated after mean-flux matching. The blue and orange shaded regions mark $2\pi/300<k<2\pi/110\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ for TNG and $2\pi/2800<k<2\pi/1000\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ for FLAMINGO, containing two and one bins, respectively. These modes are otherwise not available in training.

Figure 4: Correlation matrices of the noiseless $P_{\rm 1D}$. Top: T$$N$$G hydrodynamical, ML (N-body and 2LPT inputs) and FGPA. Bottom: FLAMINGO hydrodynamical, ML (N-body) and FGPA. Dashed brac$k$ets mark the k-bins common to both suites.

Figure 5: 1D flux bispectra, binned by mode, in the TNG (top) and FLAMINGO (bottom) test volumes, for the hydrodynamical reference, ML predictions and FGPA. The horizontal and vertical axes are the positive mode-bin centres $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ in $\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. The colour shows $B(k_{1},k_{2},-k_{1}-k_{2})$ in $\mathrm{Mpc}^{2}$, averaged over all valid Fourier-mode pairs in each $(k_{1},k_{2})$ bin satisfying one-dimensional triangle closure.

Figure 6: Connected 1D flux trispectra, binned by mode; panels as in fig. 5. The axes show the positive mode-bin centres $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ in $\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, and the colour shows the collapsed connected configuration $T_{\rm c}(k_{1},-k_{1},k_{2},-k_{2})$ in $\mathrm{Mpc}^{3}$. Each element is the connected covariance of the mode-binned powers, averaged over all positive Fourier modes in the two bins; disconnected Wick contractions, including the additional diagonal exchange term, are subtracted.

Figure 7: Distributions of $\log\tau$ in the TNG and FLAMINGO training and test volumes, with ML predictions for the test volumes. The TNG distributions are converged between 110 and $300\,\mathrm{cMpc}$. The FLAMINGO $2.8\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ box has a longer low-$\tau$ tail than the $1\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ box, which the network underpredicts, producing the deficit near $F\simeq 1$.

Figure 8: Mean-flux-matched flux statistics in the FLAMINGO $1\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ box. The solid blac$k$ curves show the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical reference, while the dashed blue curves show the prediction from the network trained on the $N544$ TNG300 simulation. The left panel compares the flux PDFs: the prediction agrees reasonably well over the intermediate-flux range but over-predicts the distribution around $F\simeq 0.8$–$0.95$ and under-predicts pixels close to the continuum. The upper-right panel shows $P_{\rm 1D}$, with the prediction-to-hydrodynamical ratio displayed below. The predicted power is within $\sim 10\%$ on scales larger than training volume but becomes progressively more suppressed toward high k. The shaded region marks $k<2\pi/(300\,\mathrm{cMpc})$, corresponding to wavelengths larger than the TNG300 training box.

Figure 9: Correlation matrices of the $P_{\rm 1D}$ in the FLAMINGO $1\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ box. The left panel shows the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical reference, while the right panel shows the prediction from the networ$k$ trained on the $N544$ TNG300 simulation. The cross-simulation prediction reproduces the weak correlations across much of the large-scale region but does not recover the hydrodynamical mode-coupling pattern accurately at smaller scales. In particular, it under-predicts the positive correlations involving the highest-k bins and introduces weak negative correlations between these bins and larger-scale modes.

2611.27151.abstract: The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest probes matter structure at $z\gtrsim2$, constraining baryon acoustic oscillations, neutrino masses, and dark matter properties. Interpreting current and upcoming spectroscopic surveys requires mock catalogues spanning Gpc-scale volumes while capturing small-scale intergalactic medium physics. This combination of high resolution and large volume is prohibitively expensive for hydrodynamical simulations. We present a field-level emulator, based on a three-dimensional U-Net, that maps approximate density and velocity fields directly to Ly$\alpha$ optical depth and transmitted flux. At $z\sim3$, we train in small volumes and test on much larger, independent ones in two settings: IllustrisTNG (training on a $110\,\mathrm{cMpc}$ box and testing on a $300\,\mathrm{cMpc}$ box with 2LPT and $N$-body inputs) and FLAMINGO (training on $1\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ and testing on $2.8\,\mathrm{cGpc}$ with $N$-body inputs). The hydrodynamical statistics of TNG and FLAMINGO differ appreciably over their common $k$-range, by $\sim15\%$ in $P_{\rm 1D}$, $\sim17\%$ in the bispectrum, and $\sim40\%$ in the connected trispectrum, although their normalized power-spectrum correlation structures remain broadly similar. Within each suite, the emulator reproduces $P_{\rm 1D}$ to $2.8\%$ in TNG and $5.6\%$ in FLAMINGO, the bispectrum to $4$--$5\%$, and the trispectrum to $10$--$16\%$, while also recovering the flux PDF and broad correlation structure. Field-level emulation thus provides a practical route to large-volume Ly$\alpha$-forest mocks for current and future surveys.

2611.27249.abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) is generally expected to suppress subhalo strong lensing through core formation, with subsequent gravothermal collapse potentially enhancing it. We show that compact stars can make a viable population of galaxy-hosting SIDM subhalos more efficient lenses than their cold dark matter (CDM) counterparts. When the baryonic potential weakens or reverses the inner velocity-dispersion gradient, SIDM halos suppress or bypass core formation, allowing inner densities to grow from early times. The evolved SIDM subhalos produce larger deflection angles and tangential caustics than in CDM. Such galaxy-hosting subhalos also dominate the galaxy-galaxy strong-lensing (GGSL) budget in clusters, yet lie far below the resolution of cosmological simulations. We calibrate a baryonic parametric SIDM model to predict their effects in the three most massive TNG300-1 clusters, finding GGSL cross sections 1.4--2.7 times those in CDM, comparable to the excess inferred in recent analyses. Baryon-enhanced SIDM lensing can thus account for the observed GGSL excess and predicts stronger perturbations from luminous satellites, testable through resolved distortions of background arcs and rings.

2611.27265.title: Features investigated: A detailed study of axion monodromy inflation using CLiENT

2611.27265.abstract: We investigate features in the primordial power spectrum from inflation, specifically those predicted by the axion monodromy model, using recent observational data. In order to compute posteriors, profile likelihoods and Bayesian evidence accurately for the complex likelihood surfaces arising in this model we have used the CLiENT emulator framework. As our data combinations we use both a "conservative" set consisting of Planck PR4 temperature, polarisation and lensing data together with DESI DR2 BAO and Pantheon+ supernovae, and a more "aggressive" set which also includes small-scale CMB data from ACT and SPT. We find no robust oscillatory feature in current data. With the conservative data the best fit lies at a frequency $\omega \simeq 51$ and lowers $\chi^2$ by 10.1 relative to a featureless spectrum. However, this feature is disfavoured by the more aggressive data combination, whose best fit lies at $\omega \simeq 31$ and lowers $\chi^2$ by 7.4. Fits to featureless data are known to give similar improvements, and the Akaike information criterion, the Bayes factors and the look-elsewhere effect all indicate that neither improvement is significant. The amplitude is limited to $A_\mathrm{osc} < 0.056$ and $A_\mathrm{osc} < 0.062$ (95%) for the two datasets. The emulators reproduce the true log-likelihood at samples of their posteriors with rms errors of 0.07 and 0.16, and the profile likelihoods are calculated with the true likelihood, using the profile capability of CLiENT.

2611.26685.abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are an extremely abundant population of red, compact, broad-line objects primarily found in the early universe. At $5<z<8$, they are at least 10 times more abundant than UV-selected quasars. Yet, how this population evolves towards lower redshift is unclear. In this work, we present our search for LRDs at cosmic noon ($2\lesssim z\lesssim 4$) in nearly 20 deg$^2$ of the Deep/UltraDeep fields of the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Combining multiwavelength wide-field imaging surveys from 0.3 to 4.5 $\mu$m, we identify 266 photometric LRD candidates. With spectroscopic follow-up from Keck/NIRES, VLT/X-shooter, and Magellan/FIRE on 24 candidates, we identify a sample of four LRDs with broad H$\alpha$ emission. With the purity of the photometric sample calibrated by spectroscopy, we estimate the number density of LRDs to be approximately $6.8\times10^{-7}$ cMpc$^{-3}$ at $2.10<z<2.55$---this is nearly a factor of 35 decrease from their flat number density evolution at $4\lesssim z\lesssim8$ estimated from JWST spectroscopic surveys. The knee of the LRD optical luminosity function also remains consistently at $M_{5500}\approx-22$ mag across $2<z<5$, below that of quasars. We further speculate that only the abundance of LRDs, but not the shape of their optical luminosity function, evolves with redshift, and the Roman Space Telescope will be able to test this decisively with a substantially larger sample of low-redshift LRDs.

2611.27611.title: Cosmological Correlators with Triple Massive Exchanges

figures.caption: Figure 1: The triple exchange diagram and its reduction. The horizontal line represents the late-time boundary at $\tau=0$, and each vertex carries an SK index $\pm$ to be summed over. The result is shown in units of $10^{-5}\lambda_{123}/H$ for four sets of mass parameters $(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})$ that share the same lightest field. The mixings $\rho_{\alpha}=(\tfrac{1}{4}+\mu_{\alpha}^{2})H/20$ offset the suppression by $1/(\tfrac{1}{4}+\mu_{\alpha}^{2})$ of each massive line and give the four sets a similar size. Since the couplings only enter through the overall factor $\lambda_{123}\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\rho_{3}$, any other choice rescales each set. Left: shape over all triangles with $k_{1}\leq k_{2}\leq k_{3}$ and $k_{1}/k_{3}\geq 10^{-4}$, as a function of $\log_{10}(k_{1}/k_{3})$ and $k_{2}/k_{3}$, from the analytical result (16) on about $10^{3}$ triangles per panel. Each panel has its own vertical and colour scale, with white at zero. The back edge of each surface is the isosceles line $k_{2}=k_{3}$, which ends at the equilateral configuration, while the front edge consists of the folded configurations $k_{1}+k_{2}=k_{3}$ for $k_{1}/k_{3}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}$ and of the isosceles configurations $k_{1}=k_{2}$ beyond. Right: the same four sets, in the same colours, along the isosceles line $k_{2}=k_{3}$ as a function of $\kappa=k_{1}/k_{3}$, from $\kappa=10^{-8}$ to the folded configuration $\kappa=2$. The dotted vertical line marks the lower end of the left panels, and the grey band the equilateral configuration. Solid lines: analytical result (16). Dots: numerical integration of (9), which agrees with the analytical result to numerical precision. Dashed lines: leading squeezed limit (37)-(38), drawn over the whole range to show where it sets in. Dotted black line: the same limit for equal masses from the closed form (42)-(45). For equal masses, the signal oscillates in $\log\kappa$ at a single frequency with a constant amplitude. For different masses, each field contributes an oscillation at a frequency set by its own mass, and their superposition is a modulated oscillation: the closer the masses, the deeper and the slower the modulation.

2611.27611.abstract: Among all tree-level contributions to the primordial bispectrum, the triple exchange of massive scalars is the most challenging. In this paper we present an analytical formula for this bispectrum in the form of a double series, which allows the three exchanged fields to have different masses and converges throughout the whole physical region. We obtain it by expanding the mixed propagator with the softest momentum, so that the triple exchange becomes a sum of integrals over two mixed propagators. Each of these integrals satisfies a differential equation and is fixed by its value at equal momentum. We further show that the squeezed limit follows directly from this formula and takes a simple and compact form.

2611.27986.abstract: We show that Warm Little Inflation is anomalous, lacks a suitable inflaton potential, and cannot sustain the thermal bath, as the quasi-static approximation over-estimated the dissipated power. To address these issues, we propose a new friction mechanism and new anomaly-free models based on one fermion charged under a U(1) gauge group in one extra dimension. The four-dimensional lattice version is a ring of $N$ U(1) groups with one fermion at each site, reducing to an anomaly-free version of the warm little inflaton model for $N=2$. The inflaton is a Wilson line, protected for $N\ge5$. Large $N$ allows a suitable monodromy inflaton potential. In the continuum limit, $N\to\infty$, the inflaton velocity becomes a five-dimensional electric field and friction becomes Ohmic dissipation, which seems able to sustain warm inflation compatibly with observations.
